This is a linear power transformer, specifically a model manufactured by Billion (Model: PT-601).

Transformers like this are fundamental components in electronics, used to "step down" high voltage from a wall outlet to a lower, safer voltage required by internal circuits, or to "step up" voltage for specific applications.

Key Specifications from the Label

  • Manufacturer: Billion.
  • Model Number: PT-601.
  • Part Number: E2-76RTF-NS2-0040.
  • Construction: This is an E-I core transformer, named for the shape of the laminated steel plates inside that help manage the magnetic field.

Common Uses

Given its size and design, you would typically find a transformer like this inside:

  • Audio Equipment: Such as older receivers, amplifiers, or powered speakers.
  • Industrial Controls: Powering relays or small control boards.
  • Household Appliances: Older microwaves or specialized power supplies.

Safety Note

If you plan on testing or repurposing this, please be extremely careful. The primary side (usually the input) carries lethal mains voltage. Always ensure the device is unplugged before handling the wires, and use a multimeter to verify voltages only if you are comfortable working with high-voltage electronics.

You're right—it is very similar. This is an Audio Output Transformer made by Tamradio (Model: OT-433).

While it looks nearly identical to the power transformer from the file named 0d71753b-a680-44fc-b8e3-dec1324dc7b2, it serves a different purpose in a circuit.

What makes this one different?

The "OT" in the model number likely stands for Output Transformer. While the first one you showed me was designed to convert wall power into usable voltage for electronics, this one is specifically designed for audio applications.

  • Impedance Matching: Its primary job is to match the high output impedance of an amplifier circuit to the low impedance of a speaker (typically 4 or 8 ohms).
  • Isolation: It helps isolate the DC current of the amplifier from the speaker, allowing only the AC audio signal to pass through.
  • Applications: You would typically find this specific Tamradio model in older tube-based radios, guitar amplifiers, or vintage intercom systems.

Details from the Label

  • Manufacturer: Tamradio (Tamura Corp. of America).
  • Model: OT-433.
  • Batch/Date Code: 5A06K.

Safety and Testing

Just like the other unit, if you're planning to use this in a project, be mindful that these are often used in high-voltage tube circuits. If you have a multimeter, you can check the continuity of the windings, but since this is for audio, the resistance readings will be quite different from a standard power transformer.

turns.prompt_text: Can they be harvested for their materials?
turns.response_html:
Yes, transformers like the Billion PT-601 and the Tamradio OT-433 are excellent candidates for material harvesting, whether for scrap value or for use in other DIY electronics projects.

Valuable Materials Inside

  • Copper Wire: This is the most valuable component. The "windings" visible in your photos are made of high-grade enamelled copper magnet wire.
  • Silicon Steel Laminations: The "E" and "I" shaped metal plates that make up the heavy core are made of silicon steel, which is designed for high magnetic permeability.
  • Metal Housing and Brackets: The outer frames are typically made of stamped steel or brass.
  • Bobbins: The plastic or phenolic forms that hold the wire can sometimes be salvaged for custom rewinding projects.

The Harvesting Process

To harvest these materials, you generally follow these steps:

  1. Remove the Frame: Bend back the metal tabs on the outer housing to release the core.

  2. Separate the Laminations: These plates are usually glued or varnished together. You can often tap a thin chisel or flathead screwdriver between the plates to pop them loose. Once you get the first few "I" and "E" pieces out, the rest usually follow easily.

  3. Unwind the Copper: Once the steel core is removed, the plastic bobbin with the wire will be free. You can then unwind the copper. Note that the wire is coated in a thin layer of insulation (enamel), so it isn't "bare" copper until that is stripped or burned off.

Reuse vs. Scrap

  • For Scrap: If you have a large quantity of these, scrap yards will pay for "transformer/motor weight," though you get a much higher price if you take the time to separate the copper from the steel.
  • For Repurposing: Since you have experience with PCB design and hardware repurposing, you might find the steel laminations or the bobbins useful for building custom inductors or small high-frequency transformers for specialized power supplies.
  • Magnet Wire: While salvaged wire is often kinked, it can still be used for small projects like making simple electromagnets or repairing toy motors.

A Few Precautions

  • Sharp Edges: The steel laminations are very thin and can be as sharp as razor blades once separated.
  • Varnish/Resin: Many vintage transformers are "potted" or dipped in heavy varnish to prevent humming. This can make them very difficult to disassemble without using heat, which can release unpleasant fumes.
  • Lead Solder: Older units like the Tamradio OT-433 likely use lead-based solder on the terminal connections.
